description: Spice trade, sea routes and the technology that sent Spain and Portugal westward.
content_html:
Europe on the Eve of Exploration

In the late fifteenth century, European merchants were hungry for the spices of Asia — pepper, cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves. These goods were not luxuries; they preserved food, masked the taste of spoiled meat and were worth their weight in silver. The problem was distance. Overland routes to Asia ran through the heart of the Ottoman Empire, whose sultans taxed or disrupted Christian merchants at will. The fall of Constantinople in 1453 intensified the pressure to find an alternative route.

Key Fact

The fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks in 1453 blocked reliable overland trade to Asia and gave Spain and Portugal a powerful economic motive to find sea routes instead.

The Rivalry Between Spain and Portugal

By the 1480s, two Iberian kingdoms had emerged as the dominant maritime powers. Portugal had been exploring the African coast since the 1420s under the guidance of Prince Henry the Navigator (1394–1460), who sponsored systematic voyages down the African coast. Castile (soon united with Aragon to form Spain under Ferdinand and Isabella) was a latecomer but equally determined to find its own route to Asia. This rivalry shaped the age of exploration.

In 1494, the two powers signed the Treaty of Tordesillas. An imaginary north–south line was drawn through the Atlantic, roughly 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. Portugal was allocated territory to the east of the line (giving it access to Africa and Asia); Spain was allocated territory to the west (opening the Americas). The treaty formalised a partnership in colonialism that would define the next century.

Prince Henry never sailed on the voyages he sponsored, but he transformed Portugal into a maritime power. He established a school of navigation at Sagres (or near it — the exact location is debated), attracted astronomers, cartographers and pilots, and commissioned systematic voyages along the African coastline. By the time he died in 1460, Portuguese sailors had reached as far south as Sierra Leone. His initiative gave Portugal a head start of several decades over its rivals.

The Portuguese motivation was partly commercial (finding a direct sea route to the spice markets of India and the East Indies), partly religious (spreading Christianity and countering Islam along the African coast) and partly strategic (finding Prester John — a legendary Christian king in Africa whose alliance might outflank the Ottoman Empire). These three drivers — gold, God and glory — ran through virtually every European voyage of discovery.

The Reconquista and Religious Motivation

Spain’s rulers had just completed the Reconquista — the 700-year struggle to reclaim the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule — in January 1492 when Granada fell. The same year, Ferdinand and Isabella expelled Jews from Spain and funded Columbus’s first voyage. This was not coincidence: the Catholic monarchs saw exploration as a continuation of their crusading mission. Spreading Christianity to new peoples was a genuine motive alongside economic gain, and it would powerfully shape how conquistadors justified what they did to indigenous populations.

Key Fact

Historians summarise the motives for exploration as “Gold, God and Glory”: the search for profitable trade routes, the spread of Christianity and the desire for personal fame and royal prestige.

Technological Advances

Without new technology, long ocean voyages would have been impossible. Three innovations were especially important. The caravel was a new type of ship that combined a sturdy hull for ocean conditions with lateen sails that allowed it to sail closer to the wind. Unlike traditional square-rigged vessels, the caravel could make progress even when the wind was unfavourable, making return journeys along the African coast possible for the first time.

Navigation also improved dramatically. The magnetic compass allowed sailors to maintain a bearing even when stars were hidden. The astrolabe allowed navigators to calculate their latitude by measuring the angle of the sun or Pole Star above the horizon. Together, these tools gave pilots enough confidence to leave sight of land and venture into the open Atlantic.

The astrolabe measured the angle of the sun at noon or the Pole Star at night. Because the sun’s angle above the horizon changes predictably with latitude, a navigator could compare their reading against published tables to calculate how far north or south of the equator they were. Longitude — east–west position — remained impossible to calculate accurately until the eighteenth century. Sailors in the 1490s navigated by dead reckoning: combining their known starting point, estimated speed and compass bearing to guess their position. It was imprecise, but combined with the astrolabe it was enough to cross an ocean.

Improved cartography also mattered. The rediscovery of Ptolemy’s Geography in the early fifteenth century gave European cartographers a framework for world maps. Arab and Chinese geographical knowledge was absorbed by Iberian scholars. By 1480, educated Europeans understood that the Earth was a sphere — the question was not whether a westward route to Asia was theoretically possible, but whether it was practically achievable. Columbus believed the distance was shorter than it actually was, a miscalculation that accidentally led him to the Americas.

The Route to Asia: South-East or South-West?

Portugal pursued the south-eastern route: sailing south along Africa, rounding the Cape of Good Hope and crossing the Indian Ocean to reach India. This strategy paid off in 1497–1499 when Vasco da Gama reached Calicut. Spain, blocked from this route by the Treaty of Tordesillas, had to look south-west. Columbus argued that Asia could be reached by sailing west across the Atlantic — a proposition that most informed sailors thought was wrong, not because they believed the Earth was flat, but because they knew the ocean was too wide to cross. Columbus was right that a westward route existed; he was wrong about what lay at the end of it.
exam_tip_html: When answering a “Explain a cause” question about the voyages of discovery, make sure you link your evidence to the specific cause you are explaining. For example, if you are explaining the role of technology, do not just name the caravel — explain how it made long ocean voyages possible (lateen sails allowed sailing against the wind; sturdy hull survived Atlantic conditions). For the 8-mark significance question, you must address significance both at the time and over time. The Treaty of Tordesillas matters because it shaped the exploration of the entire globe, not just the Atlantic.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • European voyages were driven by three interlocking motives: economic (finding profitable sea routes to bypass the Ottoman blockade of Asian trade), religious (spreading Christianity, especially for Catholic Spain after the Reconquista) and strategic (prestige and power for rival monarchies).
  • Portugal had a decades-long head start thanks to Prince Henry the Navigator’s programme of systematic exploration from the 1420s, but the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 divided exploration rights between Portugal (east) and Spain (west).
  • New technology — the caravel, the magnetic compass and the astrolabe — made ocean navigation possible; without them, explorers could not have left sight of land and returned safely.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the caravel that made long ocean voyages possible.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students may describe: lateen (triangular) sails that allowed the ship to sail closer to the wind / a sturdy hull capable of surviving Atlantic conditions / a shallow enough draught to navigate coastal waters. One mark for identifying the feature; two marks for a developed explanation of why it mattered for ocean voyages.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Treaty of Tordesillas, 1494.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It divided the non-Christian world between Spain and Portugal along a north-south line through the Atlantic (approximately 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands).
• It allocated territories east of the line to Portugal (Africa and Asia) and west of the line to Spain (the Americas).
• It was brokered by the Pope (Pope Alexander VI), giving it religious authority.
• It gave Spain the right to explore westward, enabling Columbus’s voyages and later the conquest of the Americas.
[2 marks per feature: 1 mark for identification, 2 marks for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of European voyages of exploration in the late fifteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Secure: Identifies and explains a cause with supporting evidence (e.g. economic motive: Ottoman control of overland routes raised the cost of Asian goods, pushing Portugal and Spain to seek sea routes; or technological: caravel and astrolabe made ocean navigation viable for the first time).
Mastering: Develops the cause fully, linking it to specific evidence and explaining the connection (e.g. the Reconquista completing in 1492 left Spanish crusading energy and military resources free for overseas expansion; Ferdinand and Isabella saw exploration as continuation of their mission to spread Christianity).
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: States a cause without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the fall of Constantinople in 1453 for European exploration.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that Ottoman control of the eastern Mediterranean disrupted or blocked trade and raised prices for spices and silk, creating an urgent economic incentive for both Portugal and Spain to find alternative sea routes; links this to specific voyages (e.g. Dias 1488, Columbus 1492).
Secure: Identifies the consequence with relevant supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Describes the fall without explaining consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Prince Henry the Navigator for the age of exploration.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (sponsored systematic Portuguese voyages down African coast; established infrastructure of navigational knowledge; reached Sierra Leone by 1460; gave Portugal a decades-long lead) AND over time (his programme made da Gama’s 1498 voyage to India possible; established the model of state-sponsored exploration copied by Spain). Developed argument with evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with supporting evidence; may lack the over-time dimension fully.
Developing: Describes what Henry did without fully analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Technology was the most important reason why European voyages of discovery became possible in the late fifteenth century.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• The caravel’s lateen sails allowed sailing against the wind, making return journeys along the African coast possible for the first time.
• The magnetic compass and astrolabe allowed open-ocean navigation by latitude even when stars were obscured.
• Improved cartography (rediscovery of Ptolemy’s Geography) gave navigators a theoretical framework.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• Economic motive (Ottoman blockade, spice trade profits) drove investment in exploration; technology was the means, not the motive.
• State sponsorship — Ferdinand and Isabella, the Portuguese crown — provided capital that technology alone could not supply.
• Religious motivation (Reconquista ethos, desire to spread Christianity) gave explorers and their backers ideological justification.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some points on both sides, limited judgement.
Emerging: Simple description of technology or motives without evaluating the interpretation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which instrument allowed sailors to calculate their latitude by measuring the angle of the sun?
What did the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divide between Spain and Portugal?
options: The non-Christian world into eastern and western spheres
The profits from the spice trade equally

knowledge_checks.q: Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored Portuguese voyages along the _____ coast from the 1420s.
The fall of _____ in 1453 intensified Europe's need for new sea routes to Asia.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Small ship with lateen sails ideal for ocean exploration
The Christian campaign to reconquer Iberia from Muslim rulers
1494 agreement dividing exploration rights between Spain and Portugal

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Ottoman Turks capture Constantinople?
What was the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)?
flashcard_questions.a: A Spain-Portugal agreement dividing the non-Christian world along a line through the Atlantic.

flashcard_questions.q: Which side of the Tordesillas line was granted to Spain?
flashcard_questions.a: The western side, giving Spain access to the Americas.

flashcard_questions.q: What feature of the caravel made sailing against the wind possible?
What did the astrolabe allow sailors to measure?
flashcard_questions.a: Their latitude, using the angle of the sun or Pole Star above the horizon.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was Prince Henry the Navigator?
flashcard_questions.a: A Portuguese prince who sponsored systematic voyages of exploration along the African coast from the 1420s.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Prince Henry the Navigator die?
What were the three motives historians call 'Gold, God and Glory'?
flashcard_questions.a: Profitable trade, spreading Christianity, and royal prestige.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Spain complete the Reconquista by capturing Granada?
What navigational problem could the astrolabe NOT solve?
Why was the Ottoman Empire an obstacle to European trade?
flashcard_questions.a: It controlled overland routes to Asia and taxed or disrupted Christian merchants.

flashcard_questions.q: Which route to Asia did Portugal pursue — south-east or south-west?
flashcard_questions.a: South-east: down the African coast, around the Cape of Good Hope, across the Indian Ocean.

glossary_terms.definition: The Islamic empire centred on Constantinople that controlled the eastern Mediterranean and blocked direct European land trade with Asia.
A 1494 agreement between Spain and Portugal, brokered by the Pope, dividing the non-Christian world: Portugal east of a line through the Atlantic, Spain west.
The centuries-long campaign by Christian kingdoms to reconquer the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rulers, completed in 1492 when Granada fell.
A small, manoeuvrable sailing ship developed by the Portuguese, with lateen sails allowing it to sail closer to the wind and survive ocean conditions.
An instrument using a magnetised needle to indicate north, allowing sailors to maintain a course even when clouds obscured the stars.
An instrument used to measure the angle of the sun or stars above the horizon, allowing navigators to calculate their latitude at sea.
